member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.MemoryStreamPool
member.summary: A ready-to-use pool of instances, aligned with P89OP's MemoryStreamPool: borrowing costs one line, and using on the borrowed stream returns it.
member.remarks:
The pool is built on the ordinary HayateOP engine, configured the way a specialized stream pool wants it: nothing is pre-created, a miss inside the pool size is served by creating a stream on demand, and the two background features a stream pool has no use for (auto-scaling, eviction) are switched off — so an idle pool holds its streams and runs no timers. Validation stays on: it is what enforces the capacity window below, on every return.
Streams are created with bytes and may grow while borrowed; a stream that comes back with a capacity outside the / window is destroyed instead of being parked, so buffers never linger larger than the configuration allows. Returned streams are reset to empty (position and length zero) before the next borrow.
Tightening the window clears the pool, matching P89OP: raising the minimum or lowering the maximum destroys every parked stream, because none of them can pass the new window. Widening keeps them.

example.code: using var stream = MemoryStreamPool.Instance.GetObject(); stream.Write(payload, 0, payload.Length); // returned to the pool at the end of the block

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.PooledMemoryStream
member.summary: A that knows the pool it came from: disposing it returns it to that pool instead of closing it, so a borrow/return pair can be written with using exactly as P89OP's PooledMemoryStream allows.
member.remarks:
Disposing a stream that sits in a hands it back through the pool's ordinary return path — validation, the capacity guard and the reset to an empty stream all behave exactly as for a manual Release — and the stream stays open: the buffer is kept alive for the next borrower, which is the whole point of pooling streams. The stream is closed for real only when the pool itself destroys it (a returned stream that failed validation — most commonly one that grew past the pool's maximum capacity — is destroyed, and the pool's destroy path calls the underlying ).
Disposal is once-per-borrow: a second of the same borrow is a no-op rather than a duplicate return, because returning the same object twice would let two borrowers share it later. After the pool has destroyed a stream, using it throws , like any closed stream.
A stream created directly (never handed out by a pool) owns nobody and behaves like an ordinary : disposing it closes it.

example.code: using var stream = MemoryStreamPool.Instance.GetObject(); stream.Write(payload, 0, payload.Length); // returned to the pool at the end of the block

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.PooledStringBuilder
member.summary: A holder that knows the pool it came from: disposing it returns it to that pool instead of dropping it, so a borrow/build pair can be written with using.
member.remarks:
While the instance is registered with a , hands it back through the pool's ordinary return path — validation and the clear behave exactly as for a manual Release. The instance itself is kept alive for the next borrower; only the pool can destroy it, and it does so when the builder grew past the pool's maximum capacity.
Disposal is once-per-borrow: a second of the same borrow is a no-op rather than a duplicate return. After disposing, the instance must not be used again — if it was already returned and re-borrowed by someone else, disposing it a second time would be a foreign return.
An instance created directly (never handed out by a pool) owns nobody: does nothing and the garbage collector reclaims it.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.SharedStringBuilder
member.summary: One shared by everyone who wants one, guarded by a single lock — the thread-safe shared builder P89OP used to ship alongside its specialized pools.
member.remarks:
There is exactly one backing builder: acquiring it blocks every other acquirer until the holder disposes, which is the deliberate trade this type makes. Where a pool hands each borrower its own builder, this type hands every borrower the builder — zero per-use allocation beyond the resulting string, at the price of serialising all users behind one lock.
The lock boundary is multi-writer, single-holder: writes from one holder at a time are serialized, and the reader's snapshot is taken under the same lock, so no writer can interleave in the middle of a snapshot and no reader can observe a half-written buffer. Hold scopes briefly and never across an await; a long-held scope stalls every other user of the shared builder.
Disposal clears the builder and releases the lock, exactly once (a second is a no-op), so the next acquirer starts from an empty builder.
